intro: Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum is Pierre Cuypers's 1885 cathedral of Dutch art: red brick, towers, and a bicycle tunnel straight through the middle. This is how a controversial building became the nation's museum.
page_title: Rijksmuseum Amsterdam: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: Pierre Cuypers won the commission for a new national museum in 1876 and spent nine years building it. His design refused to choose a style: Gothic church architecture (towers, large circular windows) fused with Renaissance civic architecture (rectangular windows, roofs, dormers), rooted in the Netherlandish transitional period he loved. The result in red brick with stone detailing was immediately controversial. Protestant critics found it too Gothic, too medieval, too Roman Catholic for a national museum. King William III reportedly refused to lay the first brick or perform the opening, declaring he would not set foot in that monastery. Cuypers built it anyway, and it opened in 1885.
sections.heading: A cathedral nobody asked for

sections.body: Cuypers organized the building as two squares, each with an atrium court at its centre. Through the central axis he cut a public tunnel with entrances at ground level, so the city could walk, and later cycle, straight through the museum. Above the tunnel on the first floor runs the Gallery of Honour, the ceremonial spine of the collection. The building also contained a library, and a separate fragment building, later branded the Philips wing, displayed the history of Dutch architecture in salvaged pieces.
sections.heading: Two squares and a tunnel

sections.body: The museum's 80 galleries now tell 800 years of Dutch art in a single chronological sweep, ending at the Night Watch. Getting there took a decade: from 2003 to 2013, Seville architects Cruz y Ortiz renovated the building under the motto 'Continue with Cuypers', stripping away parasitic ceilings and whitewash to recover the original volumes. The museum reopened on 13 April 2013. They added the Asian pavilion in the garden, merging old and new in what the project architect called silent architecture.
sections.heading: Continue with Cuypers

sections.body:
The Rijksmuseum's most famous fictional moment is a heist that never touches its walls. In Steven Soderbergh's Ocean's Twelve (2004), the crew's Amsterdam job targets Rembrandt's Night Watch, which hangs in the Rijksmuseum. The film establishes the painting's home as the prize, making the museum the off-screen anchor of the Amsterdam sequence. It is a backhanded compliment: the film needs the audience to know, instantly, that the Night Watch lives in the Rijksmuseum, because everyone does.

The building itself is a fixture of Amsterdam's visual identity, its twin-towered silhouette closing the Museumplein in countless films, series and photographs of the city. Cuypers's other great Amsterdam work, Centraal Station, shares its DNA, and the two buildings together define the 19th-century image of the capital. The museum that a king refused to open is now the building Amsterdam could not do without.
